records.name: 1Password
records.about: Trusted by more than 180,000 businesses to protect their data, 1Password gives you complete control over passwords and other sensitive business information. As an integral layer of the Identity and Access Management (IAM) stack, 1Password protects all employee accounts – even those you aren’t aware of. Give employees secure access to any app or service and safely share everything you need to work together – including logins, documents, credit cards, and more – while keeping everything else private. 1Password is easy to deploy and integrates with Azure AD, Okta, OneLogin, and Slack, so you can automatically provision employees using the systems you already trust. It’s simple to manage and fits seamlessly into your team’s workflow, so you can secure your business without compromising productivity.

updates.text: Agents are starting to do real work on our behalf. 1Password lets personal AI agents sign in and complete tasks securely without seeing or storing passwords, secrets, or credentials 🔐 With 1Password for Agents, you can securely use the credentials already protected in your 1Password vault to get more done. We’re partnering with the companies behind the agents you’re already using to make agent access secure and seamless. The 1Password for Agents platform is building with Meta Muse, SpaceX Super Intelligence Grok Bot, Anthropic ’s Claude AI , OpenAI , Town , Browserbase , Browser Use , Dana , Instinct , KERNEL , Perplexity , Ramp , Tomo , and Wajo AI , with more integrations on the way.

We’re excited to announce 1Password for Agents. 🎉 Personal AI agents are moving beyond answering questions. They can plan vacations, book appointments, manage recurring bills, prepare expense reports, and operate as your virtual chief of staff. To do these jobs, they need access to your accounts. 1Password for Agents is a platform that lets one or more personal AI agents sign in and complete tasks securely on behalf of the user without seeing or storing their passwords, secrets, or credentials. When an agent reaches a sign-in form, it verifies its identity to 1Password, and requests access to the credential stored in 1Password. If the user approves the request, 1Password directly autofills the credential in the destination site so the agent can’t see or take possession of the credentials. We’re thrilled to launch the 1Password for Agents platform, building with companies Meta Muse, SpaceX Super Intelligence Grok Bot, Anthropic ’s Claude AI , OpenAI , Town , Browserbase , Browser Use , Dana Intelligence, Inc. , Instinct , KERNEL , Perplexity , Ramp , Tomo , and Wajo AI , with more integrations on the way. ➡️Learn more: https://bit.ly/4iA0QC0

1Password has surpassed $500 million in annual recurring revenue 🚀 The acceleration is being fueled by growing adoption of our developer and AI security tools as customers secure the AI agents and workflows they build. That momentum is taking shape in two connected acts: ▶️1Password Unified Access helps businesses govern access across people, machines, and agents ▶️1Password for Agents helps people stay in control of the personal agents acting on their behalf We’re grateful to the customers who trust us to secure access for their people, agents, and machines, and to the frontier AI labs, hyperscalers, and personal AI agent providers bringing 1Password into the workflows where agents are built, deployed, and operated. updates.text: There’s apparently an upper limit for how much media we can actually consume, and it seems like we’ve just about hit it. US weekly media consumption tops out at ~26hrs/week, and has actually been in moderate decline since peak lockdown. In other words, if you’re competing for attention spans, either as a content-creator or app maker, then you’re increasingly playing a zero-sum game with your competition. Relatedly, a lot of the media growth recently has come from “background” consumption, i.e. listening/watching in your car, at your desk, or otherwise while doing something else. Put another way, in the battle for attention spans, content has resorted to doubling-up with other activities to stretch total consumable hours to something longer than 24hrs in a given day. So many apps and so much content, and yet so little time.

Marc Andreessen says individuals are adopting AI faster than organizations, and startup formation is going to skyrocket as a result: "I think many companies are not adopting AI while their employees are. And their employees are not necessarily telling the management what's happening. I'm gonna guess every single person listening to this podcast right now is thinking, 'Oh yeah, that's what I'm doing.'" "There's something about AI right now where it's much easier for the individual to adopt than it is the institution." "Some of those individuals are gonna figure out... it's now easier than ever for me to start my own business. So I think startup formation is gonna skyrocket from here."

Today's list of open roles at breakout startups and early-stage founders looking for team members, plus interesting moves lately in tech / AI: - Infinite Machine is hiring a Production Manager in Long Island City - Sola is hiring a Founding Solutions Engineer in NYC or Atlanta - Valon is hiring a Narrative and Brand Lead (Staff/Director) in NYC - Mistral is hiring a Head of Analyst Relations in NYC, Palo Alto, SF, Paris, or London - Deel is hiring a Field Marketing Events Manager, North America, remote in SF ...and more.

Marc Andreessen on the generational divide in how people receive new technology, and why it's "prime time" for 18-year-olds to grab AI and run with it: "Douglas Adams, the guy who wrote Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, had the defining description of how technology is received on a generational level... Any new technology is received three different ways by three different age cohorts." "If you're below the age of 15, it's just the natural way the world works. I've told in other settings the story of introducing my kid to ChatGPT at age seven, 'This is such a big deal because the computer answers questions.' And he's like, 'Duh.'... It's just normal." "If you're between the ages of 15 to 35, it's new, exciting, a hot field, and you might be able to make a career out of it, in which case you want to learn all the new things." "If you're above the age of 35, it's unholy and evil, and will surely overturn all existing structures and destroy society." "I think 18-year-olds right now, I mean, it's prime time to grab these new capabilities and run with them. It's gonna be creation of entirely new fields of entrepreneurship and creativity and art and everything." "The schools are banning AI or having all these controversies with it. But of course, if you're a kid, that just makes it cooler... AI is your like secret superpower that you have to like deviously figure out how to take advantage of."
The biggest risk is not being ambitious enough.

updates.text: The agent took a day to build. Getting it into production took three weeks. A model gateway, an orchestrator, observability, retrieval, a UI. Five services, five sets of credentials. The agent is the easy part. The stack around it decides whether it ships. Every one of those layers is also a lock-in decision. The best model today won’t be the best model in six months. The same goes for your orchestration framework, your observability tool and your vector store. One closed layer and you’re a release away from being stuck. 𝗕𝗲𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗻𝗲𝘅𝘁 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁, 𝘁𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗲𝗮𝗰𝗵 𝗹𝗮𝘆𝗲𝗿 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝘁𝗵𝗿𝗲𝗲 𝗾𝘂𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀: → Can I swap it with a config change? → Is it open source with a standard interface? → Can I run it next to my data? Any “no” is the layer to replace first. Aiven Runtime ships templates for the whole stack, so builders deploy it next to their data instead of wiring it together by hand. Learn about all agentic layers from our ticket agent blog: https://lnkd.in/dSzAAhrw Which layer of your agent stack would hurt most to swap out today? #AIAgents #OpenSource #DataEngineering #Aiven

Checkout slows down for customers in one region. It started right after a deploy. No dashboard covers that exact case. 𝗟𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗼𝗻: observability is a data problem, not a product category you buy as one agent + one bill. Your systems emit three shapes of telemetry. 𝗘𝗮𝗰𝗵 𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗱𝘀 𝗮 𝗱𝗶𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗯𝗮𝗰𝗸𝗲𝗻𝗱: → Metrics are numbers over time (“Is something wrong right now?”). Aiven for Metrics, built on Thanos and compatible with Prometheus. → Logs are text you search (“What went wrong, and where?”). Aiven for OpenSearch. → High-volume events (“Why is it happening, and for whom?”). Aiven for ClickHouse. 𝗧𝗿𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝘁𝗼𝗱𝗮𝘆: check your metrics store for labels that hold a device ID or request ID. Every value creates a new time series, and that is the most common way a metrics store turns slow and expensive. Move that data to ClickHouse, where customer ID, region, and build version are ordinary columns you group by in SQL. 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗱𝗲-𝗼𝗳𝗳: ClickHouse has no native alerting and no purpose-built UI. Schema design and query design land on you. Keep Aiven for Metrics for alerts and run ClickHouse alongside it. Then route it all with OpenTelemetry into Kafka. Kafka absorbs the ingest spike during an incident, and you add a destination without touching your apps. Which signal drives your observability bill right now: metrics, logs, or traces? Full breakdown from Tony Piazza: https://lnkd.in/dMWnhNtA #Observability #ClickHouse #OpenSearch #DataEngineering

Kafka Share Groups are not queues. That's the point. Apache Kafka® 4.2 shipped production-ready Share Groups (KIP-932). Most people call them "Kafka queues." The name stuck, but it hides the trade-off that makes them useful. Classic consumer groups give you strict ordering: one partition, one consumer. That guarantee is also the bottleneck. Scaling means more partitions, and every consumer change triggers a rebalance. 𝗦𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗚𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗽𝘀 𝗿𝗲𝗹𝗮𝘅 𝗼𝗿𝗱𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴. 𝗜𝗻 𝗿𝗲𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗻 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗴𝗲𝘁: → Consumers that join + leave without a rebalance storm → Acknowledgments per message, not per offset → Built-in poison pill handling Think of the ticket queue in a bank. Every message gets a number, but processing time depends on which operator picks it up. One slow customer no longer blocks the line behind them. 𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗶𝘁 𝗳𝗶𝘁𝘀: → Migrating off RabbitMQ or ActiveMQ, so you retire the legacy infrastructure → Variable-latency work, like an image topic where one user's heavy batch would hog a GPU → Consumers you scale on demand, so you pay for what the load needs 𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗶𝘁 𝗱𝗼𝗲𝘀𝗻'𝘁: workloads that need strict sequential processing. Keep keyed partitions for those. Full write-up by Olena Babenko: https://lnkd.in/deQyGp6g Which of your consumer workloads would you move to a Share Group first? #ApacheKafka #DataEngineering #OpenSource #Aiven

Nobody files a ticket for a query that got 40ms slower until it’s suddenly 4s. Connections pile up, the pager goes off, and everyone blames the database. Slow queries rarely show up as an incident. They show up as a trend nobody was watching. 𝗛𝗲𝗿𝗲’𝘀 𝗮 𝟱-𝗺𝗶𝗻𝘂𝘁𝗲 𝗳𝗶𝘅: 1. Turn on `𝘱𝘨_𝘴𝘵𝘢𝘵_𝘴𝘵𝘢𝘵𝘦𝘮𝘦𝘯𝘵𝘴` in your PostgreSQL database. 2. Give an agent a read-only role and have it pull the top 5 queries by total execution time every morning. 3. Have it post a short Slack summary with the query, call count, mean time, and one suggested next step (missing index? run `𝘌𝘟𝘗𝘓𝘈𝘐𝘕 𝘈𝘕𝘈𝘓𝘠𝘡𝘌`?). Your team sees the drift in standup, long before a customer feels it. Who on your team would notice if your slowest query got 2x slower tomorrow? Try Aiven Managed Agents: https://lnkd.in/dA_j-e6K #PostgreSQL #DataEngineering #Aiven

More users look at your dashboards and your bill keeps growing? Optimize your dashboard pipelines! Most dashboard pipelines look the same: an ingestion tool copies tables out of the app database, an orchestrator schedules the transforms, and a framework sits on top. That's three systems to run, monitor + debug, all so a dashboard can read an aggregate. A ClickHouse® refreshable materialized view collapses that. It re-runs a query on a schedule and replaces the target table. Point it at a PostgreSQL® table through the managed integration and you write no connection code and keep no credentials in your SQL. Your hourly rollup job becomes one SQL statement. 𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗶𝘁 𝗺𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀: your dashboard reads a small pre-aggregated table instead of scanning raw data, so queries stay fast and predictable as volume grows. And you have fewer things to page someone about at 2am. 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗰𝗵: each refresh reads the full source table from PostgreSQL. That's fine for small and medium tables. On large or fast-changing ones it adds load to your application database. Stream changes through Apache Kafka® with Debezium instead. Full write up: https://lnkd.in/dCjWEHiZ What are you still scheduling outside the database that SQL could handle? #DataEngineering #ClickHouse #PostgreSQL #ApacheKafka

updates.text: Your team shipped more this quarter. That doesn’t prove it shipped the right things. AI made output cheap. Tickets, docs and code all show up faster, and plenty of teams are counting that speed as progress. Deciding what’s worth building is still the hard part, and it’s where Allstacks Product Studio does its work. Reviewers focused on different concerns and pressure-test ideas before they reach engineering. The whole team works from one shared product definition, so every update reaches everyone without someone maintaining a doc on the side. With Allstacks intelligence underneath, those decisions stay grounded in your real delivery data and tied to the business goal you’re trying to move. Product Studio is free!. 👉 https://hubs.ly/Q04BKRn60

@Itamar Gilad (author of Evidence-Guided, former Gmail PM at Google) sees it every time teams measure honestly, whether through A/B tests, usage data or a look back at old roadmaps. In a lot of companies the real number is closer to one in seven. AI hasn’t fixed that. Itamar calls this moment “output maxing.” Roadmaps, PRDs, specs and code all get generated faster, the work ships, and everyone hopes it lands. “It’s launch and pray.” On the latest Stacked Sessions, he walks @Jeff Keyes through GIST (Goals, Ideas, Steps, Tasks), the framework he built from his years at Google for testing ideas before they reach delivery. His case for cheap validation alone is worth the listen. Fake door and concierge tests teach you most of what a late-stage MVP would, for a fraction of the cost. 🎧 Full episode: https://hubs.ly/Q04BqDgP0 #ProductManagement #ProductDiscovery #StackedSessions

Most PMs don’t have time or access to understand how their product’s code actually works, so every "is this buildable?" question turns into a meeting or message with an engineer. Usually the plan gets picked apart in refinement as the technical stakeholders dig into it. Product Studio is changing that. It brings codebase understanding to product managers to do better product work. → UX feedback you want to prioritize? Ask how that part of product works and what it would take to fix it. → Wondering if it's feasible? Check what already exists, what would need to change, and estimate how long it would take. → Does it align with product goals? Evaluate what shipped against what the original intent was. You walk into planning already knowing what the code allows, what your change will take, and what engineering needs to know to build it. Product Studio is free to use. Run it on the next feature you're sizing at https://hubs.ly/Q04B0dG30

PMs, did you know Product Studio can do all of this now? 👀 ✅ Ask for a chart and get one. “Show me cycle time with 50th, 85th, and 95th percentiles.” Done. No more exporting data to a spreadsheet. ✅ Stop worrying about AI messing up your Jira tickets. You see every change before it goes in, with a full diff and surgical edits instead of rewrites. Nothing is written until you approve it. ✅ Tickets come out matching your Jira or ADO setup. Custom fields included, so there’s no reformatting afterward. ✅ Skills run your recurring work for you. Save your bug triage, weekly reports, daily briefings, and customer voice analysis once, and the agent handles them from then on. ✅ Bring stakeholders in without losing control. They can view and comment, but they can’t edit the work or prompt the assistant. You get to spend less time on the busywork and more time deciding what’s worth building. Try it 👉 https://lnkd.in/edPW8f7r #ProductManagement #AI #aipm

Your AI token bill measures how much of your process nobody ever wrote down. An agent that doesn't have your process guesses at it. It gets it wrong, a human catches it in review, and you pay twice: tokens for the guess and engineer hours for the rework. records.name: Amazon Web Services (AWS)
records.about: Launched in 2006, Amazon Web Services (AWS) began exposing key infrastructure services to businesses in the form of web services -- now widely known as cloud computing. The ultimate benefit of cloud computing, and AWS, is the ability to leverage a new business model and turn capital infrastructure expenses into variable costs. Businesses no longer need to plan and procure servers and other IT resources weeks or months in advance. Using AWS, businesses can take advantage of Amazon's expertise and economies of scale to access resources when their business needs them, delivering results faster and at a lower cost. Today, Amazon Web Services provides a highly reliable, scalable, low-cost infrastructure platform in the cloud that powers hundreds of thousands of businesses in 190 countries around the world. With data center locations in the U.S., Europe, Singapore, and Japan, customers across all industries are taking advantage of our low cost, elastic, open and flexible, secure platform.

We’re committing a portion of Anthropic’s shares to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, a new wholly owned entity dedicated entirely to the public benefit. It will start off with 5% of our shares. For every 50% increase in the company’s value over a set baseline, we can contribute up to an extra 2%, subject to our board’s discretion. In total, this means that roughly 20% of Anthropic’s shares are committed to the public good. Our co-founders have already pledged to donate 80% of their equity, and around half our employees are donating a portion of their equity as part of a donation matching program we’ve run since our founding. In the post below, we share more details about our new fund. https://lnkd.in/erhUstfW

Today we’re launching the Anthropic Cyber Mission, a long-term commitment to securing the systems everyone depends on. Frontier AI models can be misused to exploit vulnerabilities, and many of the systems we all rely on remain dangerously exposed. The people who defend critical infrastructure and open-source software have decades of security experience, but have long been short on resources. The Cyber Mission is our new effort to support defenders with tools, resources, and research. For critical infrastructure, we’re starting with the Critical Infrastructure Defense Program, which brings frontier Claude models, on-site engineers, and our threat research to the companies that these operators rely on to keep their systems secure. For open-source, we’re launching OSS Scanner, a free, opt-in service that gives projects regular security scans from our most capable models. Each report includes a proof of concept, explanation, and suggested fix where available. These are part of our broader efforts to accelerate vulnerability discovery through to patching, to harden the underlying code, and make the systems we all rely upon more secure and resilient. This work will take time, and we expect the Cyber Mission to change as we, together with the public and private sector, learn what works. Learn about the OSS Scanner: https://lnkd.in/eAn3qNMz Read the full announcement: https://lnkd.in/ehJqWp_s

If you've never written database code, SELECT * FROM users is how you ask a database for everything it knows about its users. Once you have it you can filter it, sort it, and join it against anything else you've got. The web doesn't historically work that way. The web is a few dozen companies, each holding a filing cabinet, each with a receptionist posted out front. He'll read you one file at a time, but only files you can name, as fast as he cares to read, and as long as his boss allows. Nitter was a lightweight X reader that worked fine right up until X turned off the access it depended on. Every API (the "receptionist") is a business decision that hasn't been reversed yet. The walled garden problem is downstream of a simple question: how do I SELECT * FROM internet? https://lnkd.in/gPPTUuB7

SELECT * FROM internet.blogposts I gave an "Intro to AT Protocol" talk at Render ATL last week and I wanted to give people one simple idea to walk away with. Why can't you just SELECT * from the Internet? Some folks may remember the Semantic Web, which actually tried to answer that question. Some of web3 had this goal too (though they thought more about a world computer instead of a world database). The AT Protocol answers that question by building a network for data. You sync the network so that you can actually write that magical query. In fact, the Jetstream service ( https://lnkd.in/guUBv-mu ) makes it pretty easy to get all 24 billion public records on the network right now. So I'm doing the same thing in this linkedin post. The one thing to walk away with: SELECT * FROM internet.blogposts. That's what the AT Protocol does. (PS - Render stands up to the hype. Wonderful conference!)

updates.text: Our Symantec Threat Hunter team has uncovered a new frontier in cybercrime: “LLMjacking.” Recently featured by The Wall Street Journal and Bloomberg , our latest research exposes how threat actors are deploying autonomous agents to hunt down and hijack exposed Large Language Models (LLMs)—forcing victims to foot the computing bill for self-directed cyberattacks. But what makes this discovery truly stand out is the innovative approach our team took to expose it. Instead of waiting for an attack to happen, our researchers deployed an advanced AI honeypot —a decoy system built to perfectly impersonate an unprotected, internet-facing AI service. This forward-thinking strategy allowed us to draw the attackers in and capture their autonomous agent’s complete instruction set (dubbed “Skynet mode”) in a safely controlled environment. By proactively mapping how threat actors are attempting to weaponize AI and bypass safety controls, Broadcom is staying one step ahead in securing the future of artificial intelligence. updates.text: Earlier today, Cisco Talos published an advisory on two critical vulnerabilities in PHP core, the language underneath 70% of the worlds websites, including WordPress, Drupal and Magento. There are two things I want to share about this. First, brass tacks: Cisco Talos is monitoring closely, they have detection in place for our customers, and we've made rules available to the broader open-source community at no cost. Great work by the team! But second: I want every leader to notice how these were found. AI played a key role in discovering flaws that sat in code for more than a decade, and that’s going to keep happening - on both sides. The Talos team put it well: the historic habit of baking patches into the next deployment is not going to survive the AI era. I'd encourage every leader to treat this as a decision about how fast your organization can change, not as an IT ticket. This is critical information and requires quick action. Ask your team which public-facing systems run PHP, which are on unsupported versions, and what it would take to fix them this week. (The advisory is here, and worth sending to whoever runs your infrastructure: https://lnkd.in/ex7M4DX6 )

Here's how the solution comes together: - Agent observability: Splunk Agent Observability provides visibility into agent activity, tool calls, token usage, and potential security risks. - AI security and enforcement: Cisco AI Defense and DefenseClaw help apply security guardrails and enforce policies around agent actions. - Centralized governance: Cisco Cloud Control brings agent behavior, policy state, and AI workload insights into a common interface, helping teams investigate risks and apply policies across their AI fleet. From individual workstations to enterprise-wide AI infrastructure, Cisco and NVIDIA are working together to help organizations build resilient, secure AI environments. Cisco and NVIDIA are collaborating to build agentic trust by combining Cisco DefenseClaw with NVIDIA OpenShell to help enterprises secure coding agents with enforceable runtime boundaries and identity-aware security policies. Here's how they work together: - Secure runtime boundaries: NVIDIA OpenShell runs agents in sandboxes, limiting access to the files, networks, tools, and credentials each task requires. - Identity-aware policy: DefenseClaw connects sandbox controls to enterprise identities and policies, determining which agents can run and what resources they can access. - Guardrails and observability: DefenseClaw works with Cisco AI Defense to inspect prompts, tool calls, and responses, while recording policy decisions and security events for auditing. OpenShell provides the boundary. DefenseClaw provides the judgment, the policy, and the record around it. 🌈💾🎨Excited to share that the last study from my dissertation will appear at CSCW 2026. Through interviews with 15 queer artists, we explore how participants are resisting and refusing the encroachment of genAI into their art worlds. In particular, participants contrasted the deeply relational nature of queer art making (e.g., art as a gift) with the perceived anti-relationality of genAI development and use (e.g., art as an alienated commodity). Drawing on José Esteban Muñoz, we explore the deeply collective nature of queer art making contrasted with the straight logics of genAI. Queer art often subverts dominant aesthetic norms, like the camp sensibility of finding beauty in earnestly “bad” art. While our participants were primarily non-users and critics of genAI, some saw limited queer aesthetic possibilities in the glitches or strangeness of early T2I models. However, participants felt that the increasingly realistic image models straighten out this queerness. #HCI #CSCW #CSCW2026 Preprint here: https://lnkd.in/eT2_p5rH

For the research-minded — CoreStory Frontier's PATOIS study is out. The question: when an AI agent is working through a multi-step task, does it help to attach instructions to each response the system sends back? Or does the agent already know what to do? We ran 600 trials across five conditions. The answer splits cleanly in two. Tell the agent something it could never have worked out on its own — like the random string a server hands back meaning "this is where page two starts" — and it uses it every time. 30 out of 30. Leave that string out, and it fails every time. 0 out of 30. Tell the agent something any competent engineer already knows — how paging works, when to stop, when to lock — and nothing changes. The model already had it right. We also tried a stricter, more structured format for those instructions. Identical behavior, 38% more output. You pay for the formality and get nothing back. So the takeaway isn't "write longer prompts." It's narrower: send the agent the facts it cannot infer, and make everything else earn its place. Full write-up: frontier.corestory.ai

updates.text: A 2,500 GB database with a 20 GB hot working set doesn’t need 2,500 GB of RAM. Restoring a 100 TB database with Lakebase Postgres takes seconds. How? A branch-based restore is a metadata operation. updates.text: A fresh runner downloads hundreds of megabytes before any test runs. It doesn’t have to. Playwright pulls browsers, Cypress grabs its runner, pip fetches wheels every time. That’s minutes per job, and stalled downloads can fail it outright. More agents mean more jobs, more waiting, more risk. Develocity 2026.3 caches these artifacts nearby, serving pip, Playwright, and Cypress packages from a local edge node instead of the open internet. Python setup is now up to 40% faster against a cold cache. One step in GitHub Actions or Jenkins: https://lnkd.in/gimWHz9K #ShipNote #Develocity

Your agent passes the check, but bugs still slip through. More eyes on the review won't fix it. When your AI writes both the code and its own tests, a green checkmark doesn't mean it's right. It might write tests that pass for the wrong reasons, or just delete a test that was failing. Teams trust and approve passing builds and bugs slip through. With agents now pushing more code than people, the more you scale, the larger the scope of the problem. The fix? Test every change against your real regression suite, the tests your agent didn't write. Lock it from editing existing tests during a fix (it can still add new ones). Hans Dockter explains why even smarter models won't solve this: https://lnkd.in/ghgP88Ue #FromTheFounder #ContextEngineering #Develocity

Your builds pass, but they rerun every downstream test without telling you why. A cache key depends on a task's inputs. Change just two bytes in an early output, and every key downstream changes too. So tests, analysis, and packaging all run again; and since the build passes, the team doesn’t look. You pay for it on every build: in CI costs and waiting time. More agents mean more builds, so the waste compounds. A cache miss without a failure only shows up when you compare builds. Build Scan Comparison does that, it puts two builds side by side and shows exactly what input changed. That’s how we traced one issue to javac itself: it was writing the same class differently on different machines. Read the blog: https://lnkd.in/gsws-g6e #WhatWeLearned #Develocity

Your AI agents write code fast, then wait on CI. Why? Each failed build is a do-over. You pay for the compute, and the fix can't ship. A Bluesky dev captured the pain perfectly in that screenshot. Scale this up and the problem gets worse. More agents mean more changes in the queue, longer waits, bigger bills, and all that AI speed lost to idle time. The solution? Do less work each run. A build cache skips unchanged tasks so a one-line fix doesn’t rebuild everything, and test selection runs only what’s affected. See what Hans Dockter says about where the time goes: https://lnkd.in/gyGHmKDP #TheReframe #Develocity

Your AI agent is only as good as the context it can reach. If critical knowledge isn't documented, permissions block access, or instructions are cluttered with irrelevant information, agents are left to guess, and will often confidently produce the wrong result. Good context requires three preconditions: the information has to exist, the agent has to be able to access it, and what it receives has to be relevant to the task at hand. Read the full CAFE(S) paper to learn more about what good context looks like. Link in the comments.

94% of AI token consumption is now spent re-reading context. In our latest Q3 AI Impact Report, we found that cache-read tokens reached 94% of the total token mix over the past four quarters, while output tokens shrank. The data suggests AI spend is growing because the background context required to produce code is ballooning, not because models are generating more code.

Median PR size is up 122% year-over-year. Teams have more code to review and the same review capacity. Published today, our Q3 AI Impact Report points to that volume as the main reason why first reviews are taking longer. Our research team suggests two other factors that could also be slowing first reviews: 1. AI-generated changesets take more effort to review, which ties up reviewers and pushes everything else back in the queue. 2. Reviewers hesitate to pick up large, unfamiliar, or AI-generated diffs because they're worried about missing a bug that's hard to spot. Read the full findings in our Q3 AI Impact Report: https://lnkd.in/gtD3CmBe

An early finding from DX’s Q3 AI Impact Report: Teams generating high volumes of AI-authored code wait 105% longer for code reviews. Data from 500+ engineering organizations shows teams generating more than 80% AI-authored code wait more than twice as long for a first review, compared to teams writing predominantly human-authored code. records.about: Swamp is Deterministic automation for AI agents. You've asked your Agent to orchestrate a complex operation — and it does it right, most of the time. Swamp teaches your Agent to build and execute repeatable workflows, makes all the data they produce searchable, and enables your team to collaborate in a predictable way.

updates.text: Lights out (dark) factories or lights on factories? There’s a misconception that the goal with agents is full lights-out. Code written, tested, deployed, maintained... no humans needed. I don't have that same desire for it. We run a lights-out operation at Swamp for ops and reactive work. Alerts come in, the system figures out what’s going on, handles it or escalates. That works because we’ve already done the thinking about what should happen. The system knows where to stop. Product work though? A small team build Swamp, none of us write code, and we’re still arguing about what to build and how it should work. Not reviewing diffs. Arguing about whether a feature belongs, whether the approach is right, whether we’ve thought about what happens when a user hits the edge we didn’t plan for. That taste is what we care about greatly! This is why I don't want to push toward full autonomy. A ticket like “add a retry command” looks ready to go. Then you start asking whether retry means restart from scratch or resume from the failure, what happens to infrastructure the first run created, whether the workflow definition might have changed since. At agent speed those questions just become code, nobody discussed them but they shipped. I want agents doing the work. I don’t want to find out what we promised users by reading the docs after it’s built. https://lnkd.in/e-TMkFd8

Had fun talking to Techstrong TV and Mike Vizard about how to strike the balance between probabilistic LLMs and the deterministic systems that actually run reliably at scale. https://lnkd.in/g3dyrYPC It's not surprising that the first idea we had as an industry about how to build AI agents turned out to be inefficient and hard to manage. But we can do so much better now - building a corpus of re-usable behaviors that enable the interactions and automation we want, across whatever interface we want.
Welcome to the era of herding pets! Does Pets vs. Cattle apply to AI clusters? Read on... https://lnkd.in/dBWjk4SV
Happy birth day to Swamp Club ! Fortuitously, it's also my birthday as well. Gift me a few minutes of your time and read this new blog posting. 😊

I spent a long time thinking managing platform operations and infrastructure meant choosing between structure and flexibility. - Pick a rigid framework and you get reliability, until the day it can't bend to what you actually need and you're stuck. - Pick flexibility and you get duct taped scripts and lack of control. Swamp has changed my mind. It's the first thing that's given me both at once. Structure where I needed guardrails, flexibility to integrate into everything else I've needed to run a cohesive platform. Today Swamp Club raised $7M in seed funding, led by Amplify Partners, with Encoded Ventures, Jesse Robbins and Scott Tolinski also participating. I could talk about the round. I'd rather talk about what people did with it. Agentic Code review running 8x cheaper and 3x faster. A science lab. A fleet of robot arms. An entire sales pipeline. Thousands of users, 340 million+ events from people running Swamp in all sorts of wonderful ways. Saying "I'm grateful to the team and everyone that's backed us" undersells how thankful I am to everyone that has supported the journey so far. Read about it here: https://lnkd.in/eHCecQ32 Come build with us.

Happy Ada Lovelace Day! Ada Lovelace is often considered the world's first computer programmer. And what's crazy is that she was writing instructions for a computer back in 1843, before a working programmable computer ever even existed. Charles Babbage, a mathematician, was designing a mechanical computer, and Ada wrote an algorithm showing how that same computer could be used to calculate Bernoulli numbers. And although the machine was never completed, she was already exploring what programming and computers could become nearly 100 years before modern computers existed. https://findingada.com

updates.text: Before an agent acts on your behalf, four things should already be true: a rule allows the action, the authority behind it is current, a failure has a defined path, and the decision will be recorded. If any of the four is missing, you have a demo, not a deployment. Which one does your team find hardest? forgeorbital.com

Deterministic code, not another model, should decide whether a high-consequence agent action is allowed, blocked or held for review. Models can explain themselves. Controls have to live outside them. That is how Forge Orbital works: the check sits in front of the action, and the outcome is recorded. Where does the control live in your agent workflows? forgeorbital.com

A log line tells you something happened. A recorded decision tells you why it was allowed. The difference matters six months later, when a reviewer asks for the rule, the evidence the agent saw, and the person who held authority. Forge Orbital keeps that record, and it verifies offline. Which of those three could you reproduce right now? forgeorbital.com

Most agent failures are not model failures. They are authority failures: nobody can say which rule allowed the action or who had the standing to approve it. Forge Orbital is the accountability engine for AI agents: an independent check runs before the action, and every decision lands in a recorded trail a reviewer can replay. What would your team be able to show an outside reviewer today? forgeorbital.com

A useful test before any agentic AI deployment: seven questions, and none of them are about the model. Brittany Istenes, our Chief Ecosystem Officer, lays out the questions that decide whether an agent can be trusted inside a regulated workflow: who authorized each action, which rule allowed it, what happens when it fails, and whether you can replay the decision afterward. The Seven Questions Every Enterprise Should Ask Before Deploying Agentic AI: https://lnkd.in/gTnTcH4J

updates.text: Accessibility Assistant for Figma v53: From Design Decisions to Handoff https://lnkd.in/gvNRu7Qb In an internal analysis of accessibility bugs, a colleague found that roughly half could be traced back to design decisions. These were issues we should have caught earlier, before those decisions became codified in code and long before anyone encountered them in a shipped product. That’s one of the reasons I started working on Accessibility Assistant for Figma. I wanted to help designers catch issues while they worked and help them build their accessibility knowledge along the way. Version 53 brings more of that work together, organizing annotations, assessments, issues, and handoff around projects.
While only for one day, looking forward to returning to Toronto Friday for the a11yTO - Accessibility Toronto Conference.

Not every WCAG violation should stop a launch. But some defects absolutely should. An unlabeled “Submit” button is a tiny technical flaw. It’s also the difference between someone buying your product and walking away. Conformance and user impact measure different things, so I use one question as the release gate: Can a person with a disability independently complete the same critical task as everyone else? If yes, ship it and prioritize the fix immediately. If no, it’s a blocker. Hold the release. Block every violation and you stall delivery over issues that barely touch users. Ignore severity and you lock people out of checkout, login, or the application they came to submit. My latest article offers a five-level severity scale and a blocker checklist covering keyboard access, screen readers, forms, custom components, error recovery, and mobile. https://lnkd.in/gv4Bv9s3 #Accessibility #DigitalAccessibility #WCAG #ProductManagement #QA #InclusiveDesign #A11y

Web accessibility in France and Sweden: same principles, different ways of putting them into practice 🇫🇷 🇸🇪 After 8 years working in web development and accessibility in France, I moved to Sweden this year to continue working in digital accessibility. One thing I’m discovering is that sharing the same European accessibility principles doesn’t mean working within the same framework. France and Sweden have different national legislation, testing methodologies, reporting requirements and approaches to oversight. Understanding these differences matters, especially for companies operating across borders. The technical principles may be familiar, but the way we turn them into everyday practice can be very different. I’ve written an article for a11yblog.com exploring what’s the same, what’s different, and what we can learn from both countries. Read the full article here: https://lnkd.in/dxMeiRQn I would be happy to hear from accessibility professionals working in France and Sweden: what differences have you noticed? #WebAccessibility #A11y #DigitalAccessibility #InclusiveDesign #Legislation #RGAA #InclusiveDesign #WCAG #France #Sweden

Solana’s biggest core protocol change since launch goes live on mainnet tomorrow. Alpenglow replaces Solana ’s consensus protocol on Wednesday, October 21. Finality is designed to drop from seconds to roughly 150 milliseconds, putting Solana in range of traditional payment rails. Galaxy has been testing it since the early days. Here’s what changes and what doesn’t: → Consensus: Alpenglow replaces how the network reaches agreement on blocks → Speed: finality is designed to drop to roughly 150 milliseconds → Staking: nothing changes in how stake earns rewards → Validator costs: validators now pay a flat, lower fee to vote Galaxy has run a validator on the Alpenglow community test cluster since June 2026, and on testnet and devnet since activation there. updates.text: Our newest frontier model, Gemini 4 Argon, is accelerating scientific discovery. Here's how researchers are using it to drive breakthroughs in fusion, biology, and quantum computing: ⚛️ In nuclear fusion, Argon helped discover a broader class of counterexamples to Grad's conjecture — a nearly 60-year-old assumption in plasma physics — creating new benchmarks for stellarator 3D magnetic fields. 🧬 In biology, it designed five novel, lab-verified serine esterases in a matter of hours — enzyme engineering that would previously have taken months. This work demonstrates the potential for rapid acceleration in fields such as biomanufacturing, green chemistry, and drug development. 🩺 In rare disease research, scientists at Gamow Labs used Argon to analyze de-identified genomes from newborns with rare developmental lung disorders — pinpointing a chromosomal rearrangement that routine software missed for years, and explaining why it went undetected. 🧮 In quantum computing, Argon translated our AlphaQubit error-correction decoder into a single optimized hardware kernel — nearly doubling inference throughput — and cut spacetime costs for a key quantum subroutine by more than 100x. updates.text: #News for #Investors and #Media : Today, we presented longer-term late-breaking data, marking encouraging progress for people living with ovarian cancer. #ESMO2026 Learn more: https://gsk.to/4yFy0Fd

It’s not just about treatment; it’s about understanding the disease behind it. Around 420,000 women are diagnosed with Endometrial cancer every year, and while precision medicine is potentially transforming care, advanced disease remains harder to treat. That’s why we’re investing in biology, translational science and advanced data to match the right targets to the right modalities and test potential new medicines where current options are limited. Learn more 👇 #ESMO2026

A lung cancer diagnosis can come as a shock and leave you with more questions than answers. Biomarker testing helped Juanita better understand her cancer and navigate what comes next. Watch the full video here 👉 https://lnkd.in/edmchmMx #ESMO2026

Cancer research is entering a new era. Advances in cancer biology, technology and drug development are creating opportunities that simply weren't possible a decade ago. The challenge now is translating those advances into medicines that can potentially improve outcomes for the patients who need them most. At #ESMO26 , the focus will shift to the latest data. GSK will share more than 20 abstracts this year, reflecting the momentum across our solid tumor portfolio and the ambition driving our Oncology R&D organization. For me, the more important question is what these findings tell us about cancer biology, and how we use that understanding to develop better medicines for patients. In a new custom content article for STAT ahead of #ESMO26 , I share more on what it takes to move from scientific opportunity to clinical progress, and why focused development choices will define the next phase of oncology R&D. I look forward to the conversations in Madrid and to the science that will continue shaping the future of oncology. Read the STAT article here: https://bit.ly/4ze0eb2

Chronic hepatitis B is a viral infection that affects the liver and often has no symptoms, especially in its early stages. Because it can go undetected, many people are unaware they are living with the condition until liver damage has already occurred. Understanding the condition is key to improving diagnosis and outcomes. 🎥 Watch the video to learn what CHB is, how it develops, and why early detection matters.

records.about: The InnerSource Commons Foundation is a community of industry professions and researchers founded to promote InnerSource - the application of Open Source principles and practices in enterprises. Come join us to learn about best practices on how to leverage Open Source principles to enhance cross-team collaboration within your company and gain efficiency and build open source skills enabling you to meaningfully participate in open source communities. InnerSource Commons Vision The InnerSource Commons is a thriving community that empowers organisations and people worldwide to apply and gain the benefits of open collaboration in their internal work. Founded in 2015, the InnerSource Commons is now supporting and connecting over 3000 individuals from over 750 companies, academic institutions, and government agencies. The InnerSource Commons Foundation was incorporated on February 19th, 2020 and is now a 501(c)(3) public charity. InnerSource Commons Mission We empower developers and organisations to apply open collaboration principles in their daily work. We are the neutral hub and central collaboration space for InnerSource knowledge. As such, we maintain our independence and operate on a lean budget. We build a strong, inclusive community and industry partnerships. Together, we apply open collaboration principles to drive the conversation about InnerSource and steward the InnerSource body of knowledge.

updates.text: Agent skills keep turning out to be one of the biggest levers affecting AI coding output... and also one of the most overlooked. As of September, almost half of the developer-weeks we track in Jellyfish had essentially zero (!!) skill use. This is especially crazy given how strongly skill use correlates with high levels of coding output. (WAY more than what model or harness you use.) In this clip from my AI Engineer NYC talk, I get into how much heavy skill use actually moves output. (Full talk out soon!)

The typical software engineering leader has MAJOR trust issues with 20% of their development team right now. These "developers" can write code, but they aren't trusted to be the solo reviewer on other people's work and definitely can't approve a merge. Obviously we're talking about AI coding agents 🙂 Five years ago this would have been insanity, but now that's the reality at most AI-assisted software orgs. In the Jellyfish data, coding agents now author 22% of PRs at the median company, but only 0.6% of PRs get merged without a human review. This is the source of the massive "review bottleneck" everyone is talking about. I wrote a piece for Tessl about why this bottleneck is really an ROI problem, and what the top companies are doing to build trust in their agents faster. https://lnkd.in/gunA8FPg I’ll be getting into all of this and more in my talk “Botsitting Doesn’t Scale” at AI Native Dev Con in NYC, Nov 2–4. Come join me!

🥁 The most used agent skill is...Code Review! In the recently released September AI Engineering Trends report, Jellyfish Research measured invocations of agent skills in Cursor and categorized them by use-case using an LLM. The data below shows the distribution of skill categories invoked by engineers within Cursor in the past month. This captures the current state of AI development practices and the specific workflow steps engineers are augmenting within the AIDLC. Compiled from 1,300+ companies, 294K engineers, 105M PRs, the results of the largest study of its kind comprise real-world engineering signals about how organizations and developers are using AI tools across the SDLC. You can access the full data to benchmark your organization’s AI adoption and usage maturity here: https://lnkd.in/geGvmh7k #AIEngineering #AIEngineeringTrends #AIData #AgentSkills #CodeReview

Most 2027 AI budgets are built on an assumption the data doesn’t support: that AI spend behaves like headcount. 💰 An engineer costs about the same in month twelve as in month one. But AI spend per engineer doesn’t. It compounds, it jumps and what each extra dollar buys depends on the size of your org. Swipe through the first finding from our new Jellyfish Research guide. The typical company’s AI spend per person roughly tripled in six months, and it rarely held steady from one month to the next. The full guide has three more findings, plus a five-step exercise to plot your own team on the curve before you commit to a number. Get the guide: https://lnkd.in/eeXXzqHR #EngineeringLeadership #AIinEngineering #EngineeringBudget #AnnualPlanning #BudgetPlanning #AISpend

If you and your team are arguing about the right frontier model for software development, you can stop now – we've seen in the Jellyfish data that it mostly doesn't matter 🙂 Example: check out this clip from my AI Engineer NYC talk. This summer, when Cursor changed its defaults, a huge number of engineers got switched from other models to Grok very quickly... and their output basically didn't change. What does matter? I'm glad you asked, that's what the rest of the talk is about! I'll post it as soon as it goes live (hopefully this week).

Yesterday I spent 6 hours with 50 leaders across institutional real estate talking about AI. This was part of the inaugural NAREIM Innovation Summit. While the detailed conversations are always confidential at NAREIM, a few themes emerged that are worth sharing: 1. We have moved from AI being a novelty to driving NOI 2. The technology is the worst it will ever be today and it's already capable of executing some of the most complex and nuanced tasks 3. Changing behaviors is far more difficult than changing technology - people across the board are very resistant to change 4. Leadership MUST come from the top. To get your organizations onboard, you can't outsource the leadership 5. Selecting the right partner is critical. It's never been easier to spin up a AI first X or Y - but choosing partners that understand your business, your industry and the nuances and context of your asset class is critical 6. GP's should not build out large tech teams and try to build their own. LP's want GP's to differentiate on investment outcomes, not technology spend. 7. AI can get expensive.. fast if you don't understand and have the right guardrails 8. We have moved beyond the chat era to the agentic era and those in the room learned how to build their own agents (very cool workshop) 9. Embrace those people in your org that are leaning into AI - give them the opportunity to coach and lead your org. 10. Embrace curiosity. We are all being forced to reimagine our businesses and to do that you need to be curious and go back to first principles. The private markets are at a structural inflection point and the convergence of AI and investment management is happening fast. It's no longer a novelty and it's exciting to see a room full of leaders embrace the opportunity to learn and grow... together.

updates.text: More workers have access to paid leave than ever before, but millions still cannot take the time off they need to care for children, aging parents or other family members. **Special Biannual Report** 🔹 Access to paid leave has increased, but large gaps remain. The share of workers with access increased to 71% in 2024-25 from 66% in 2017-18 and 60.2% in 2011. Yet only 62.6% of workers in the bottom quartile of earners had access, compared with 90.9% in the top quartile. 🔹 Caregiving is a main reason workers take leave. Nearly 14% of all leave during an average week was for family medical care, childcare, eldercare or the birth/adoption of a child. That translates to around 4.5 million adults. Nearly one in five workers aged 35-44 who took leave cited caregiving. 🔹 Broader access has not closed the caregiving gap. Among workers with paid leave, more than one in five could not use it for childcare (22.4%) or eldercare (21.9%). That is more than five times the 4.2% who could not use it for their own illness or medical care. 🔹 Unmet leave needs remain widespread. In an average month, 12.3 million workers needed leave but did not take it. 🔹Women and prime-age workers bear much of that burden. Women accounted for nearly three-fifths of workers who needed leave but did not take it and were nearly twice as likely as men to cite childcare or eldercare as a reason. Prime-age workers accounted for 70.4% of unmet leave needs; 44.8% of Millennials aged 35-44 cited caregiving. Access to leave has expanded over the past decade. More workers are taking paid or unpaid time off. Yet millions still cannot take the leave they need, with large gaps concentrated around caregiving. Those gaps will become more consequential as the population ages and strain in the formal care sectors shifts more responsibility onto families. Without more flexible and usable leave, caregiving demands will continue to constrain labor force participation and productivity, especially among prime-age workers. That creates a growing headwind for employers and the broader US economy.

updates.text: Lantern is headed to GitHub Universe next week! Our team will be onsite in San Francisco, connecting with clients, partners, and the broader GitHub community. We’re looking forward to conversations around GitHub, AI, modern software development, and what’s next for teams building with more speed, clarity, and confidence. Will you be there? Let’s connect.

The faster AI moves, the more valuable it becomes to slow down and talk. I was reminded of that in a candid conversation today about where enterprise AI is headed. No grand predictions. Mostly leaders comparing notes on increasingly difficult questions. ❔How do you move from experimentation to scale? ❔How do you govern AI without slowing innovation? ❔How do you know where to invest? ❔...and ultimately, how do you know whether AI is actually creating value? That last question keeps bringing me back to AI economics. As AI moves deeper into workflows and agents, the conversation needs to move beyond licences, tokens and even time saved. 👉 AI should increasingly be managed as variable enterprise capacity, not simply as an incremental technology cost. 👉 This is where architecture, finance and governance meet. The more important question is: where should we allocate intelligence, and what business outcome are we getting in return? That could mean greater capacity, faster cycle times, better quality, lower risk or new growth. The point isn’t simply to make AI cheaper. It’s to understand where human and machine intelligence can create the most meaningful value, then keep learning and reallocating from there. The most interesting takeaway had nothing to do with economics. When everyone feels pressure to move faster, leaders need space to compare notes honestly, challenge each other, and admit that nobody has all the answers yet. Technology is accelerating. Human connection may matter more because of it. And no, we didn’t solve enterprise AI over lunch. Microsoft Lantern #AIModernization #AITransformation

People often ask why I'm so passionate about our #EarlyCareer hiring program at Lantern . Here's the answer: 1. #AI -native mindset. Companies today have three worker types: (A) people who are learning to adopt AI in the workplace (the majority), (B) people who are too far along in their career to bother (a minority), and (C) people who can't contemplate doing high-quality work without AI (future leaders). A workforce filled with diverse perspectives always outperforms, and so at a time when tech-industry job postings for early career talent are at an all-time low, I'm in the market for the top 1% of category Cs to join my terrific team of category As. 2. It's time for #LearnItAlls to shine. Aspiring young workers have high curiosity and a fast metabolism to consume new learnings. Frankly, it’s a matter of survival in the early stages of one’s career. And you know what? It’s contagious. These days, many of our clients are re-thinking their business operating model and entire industries are asking, “why did we even do it like this in the first place?". Status quo is the enemy. Meanwhile, the pace of technology innovation is mind-numbing, which rewards "learn-it-alls" much more than "know-it-alls". I believe a healthy mix of seasoned subject matter experts and fast learners is the ideal combination for the #EraOfAI . 3. An outlet for #Mentorship . Lantern has an extraordinary team of technology subject matter experts, industry veterans, and true career advisors — some of the very best in class. I believe people with lots of experience are at their best when they share knowledge with others in the flow of business. The old Robert Heinlein quote "When one teaches, two learn" applies widely at Lantern, and mentorship quickly (and sometimes surprisingly!) becomes a two-way street. Every accomplished leader in the industry today benefited massively from acts of mentorship, big and small, throughout their careers. Lantern leaders "pay it forward", usher in the next generation of top talent, and enjoy every bit of it along the way. I'm inspired by the gifted, early career employees who have survived bootcamp the last two years and are now thriving at Lantern. I channel your passion often and I’m excited to see you realize your career potential in the years ahead. Godspeed! #TeamLantern #LearnItAll #InspiredTeams

Congratulations to this year's winners: • Woamy : Making a recyclable cellulose-based biofoam that replaces plastic foams used in protective packaging. • ZCJ: Creating a new way to develop steel through a low-carbon process. And congratulations to this year's distinguished honorees: • Virenti : Offering a bio-based PCB laminate, as an alternative to oil-based laminates, made from wood-derived materials, manufactured using a toxic-chemical-free process. • EzyGreenPak : Providing plant-based, water-soluble, biodegradable non-woven bags as a plastic-free packaging alternative. • DEScycle : Developing a low-impact e-waste recycling solution for metals, removing the need for smelting and providing a closed loop recycling option for metals to be reintroduced to the supply chain. For more about this year's winners, the Future Positive Challenge, and an update on our ongoing projects with past winners, see here: https://logi.link/9cc6a1

Designing a sleek, durable, high-performance mouse or keyboard is tough. Designing one that can be easily opened, repaired, and reassembled by a non-expert with standard tools? That’s next-level engineering. This International Repair Day, we’re sharing a look at how our product teams approach designing with repair and longevity to the forefront: ⬜ Visible, standard screws: Limiting adhesive and prioritizing accessible fasteners so users can safely open devices. ⬜ Modular components: Isolating wear-and-tear parts like batteries, switches, and glides so they can be easily replaced or upgraded ⬜ Genuine replacement parts: Partnering directly with iFixit to provide OEM spare parts and multilingual step-by-step repair guides. By integrating repairability into our product design approach, we’re expanding the repair options available to our customers. Check out our latest FY26 Impact Highlights Report to see how design choices drive measurable environmental impact: https://lnkd.in/gKkS_JcC #Engineering #ProductDesign #CircularDesign #DesignforSustainability #InternationalRepairDay #Logitech

updates.text: Hace 27 años empezamos a transformar el comercio y los servicios financieros en América Latina con un propósito claro, una estrategia consistente y la convicción de seguir construyendo valor en el largo plazo. Hoy, esa visión se refleja en la escala y el crecimiento de nuestro ecosistema. En el segundo trimestre de 2026 alcanzamos US$10,2 mil millones en ingresos netos, un 50% más que hace un año, y llegamos a 89 millones de compradores únicos, un 26% más que en el mismo período de 2025. Por su parte, Mercado Pago alcanzó los 88 millones de usuarios activos mensuales, lo que representa un crecimiento interanual del 30%. Estos resultados reflejan nuestras inversiones estratégicas y el trabajo de más de 130 mil personas que no se conforman, dan el máximo y ejecutan con excelencia para generar cada vez más valor a nuestros usuarios. Seguimos democratizando el comercio y los servicios financieros para transformar la vida de millones de personas en América Latina. Lo mejor está llegando. 🚀 #OrgulloMELI

Mercado Pago, entre las principales fintech del mundo 🌎 Mercado Pago fue reconocido en el ranking World's Top Fintech Companies 2026, elaborado por CNBC y Statista que evalúa a más de 3.500 empresas en todo el mundo. Este reconocimiento refleja el impacto que estamos generando para democratizar los servicios financieros en América Latina. En los últimos 12 meses Mercado Pago procesó cerca de US$307 mil millones en volumen de pagos y superó los 80 millones de usuarios activos mensuales, impulsando además el acceso al crédito para miles de pequeñas y medianas empresas de la región. Este reconocimiento es un reflejo de cómo seguimos construyendo soluciones que simplifican la vida de millones de personas y potencian el crecimiento de quienes emprenden y hacen negocios en América Latina. #OrgulloMELI

El Mundial terminó con un hito histórico para el Fixture 2026 de Mercado Pago, que ingresó al Guinness World Records™ al superar la mayor cantidad de personas haciendo pronósticos deportivos en un mes. Esta experiencia gratuita nos permitió conectar y compartir la pasión por el fútbol con más de 25,2 millones de hinchas de Brasil, Argentina, México, Chile y Uruguay que realizaron casi 1.000 millones de pronósticos durante el torneo. En MELI el partido continúa. Sigamos dando el máximo, ejecutando con excelencia y compitiendo en equipo para ganar en cada jugada.💛 #OrgulloMELI

En Mercado Libre, el trayecto lo construyes tú. Nadie te lo regala. El desarrollo no es casualidad: es el resultado de elegir ser protagonista de tu propio trayecto, cada día. El esfuerzo se ve, se reconoce y se premia. Acompaña a Giovana, Aldair y Nico, talentos de nuestra operación logística, y descubre cómo pasaron de su primer día como Auxiliares de Almacén a liderar uno de los equipos más grandes de América Latina. El ritmo no para. La operación no espera. Lo que haces con ellas define tu trayecto.

Ya está disponible una nueva edición de Inside Mercado Libre, nuestro podcast para inversores. En este episodio conversamos con André Chaves, Senior VP and Country Head de Mercado Pago Brasil, sobre la estrategia, las ventajas competitivas y el potencial de crecimiento de Mercado Pago en el país. La conversación también aborda los pilares de la propuesta de valor que llevaron a Mercado Pago a liderar el NPS en Brasil, tanto en banking como en adquirencia, y cómo nuestra base de clientes está evolucionando hacia segmentos más elevados. Además, se comenta el potencial transformador de la IA en crédito, prevención de fraude y educación financiera. 🎧 Puedes escucharlo aquí: https://lnkd.in/dcxpwE4D #OrgulloMELI

updates.text: Think you need a computer science degree to work at a tech company? Maybe you're in the trades right now, wondering whether that experience counts. It does. The people running Meta's Cheyenne data center came from electrical work, commissioning, food manufacturing, and industrial controls. Here's how they got here. 👇 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘄𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗱𝗼𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗯𝗲𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗠𝗲𝘁𝗮, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗱𝗶𝗱 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗸 𝗮 𝘁𝗲𝗰𝗵 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗮𝗻𝘆 𝘄𝗮𝘀 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗻 𝗮𝗻 𝗼𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻? Most of this team counted themselves out before they applied. The technical foundation built in trades and industrial settings — PLCs, automation, troubleshooting complex systems under pressure — maps directly onto data center work. "I always thought working at a tech company was outside of my reach. But the controls experience I built at Smucker's translates directly. PLCs, automation, troubleshooting complex systems — that's exactly what a data center needs. You don't have to be a software engineer to work at Meta." — Rafael, Critical Facility Engineer (former controls tech, food manufacturing) 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗱𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝗰𝗮𝗿𝗲𝗲𝗿 𝗴𝗿𝗼𝘄𝘁𝗵 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗹𝗼𝗼𝗸 𝗹𝗶𝗸𝗲 𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲? Growth isn't gated by title or tenure. Engineers here are building software tools, automating workflows, leading AI adoption, and stepping into leadership, often within their first year. "Transitioning into the data center industry with Meta has given my career an incredible new trajectory and opened up continuous professional development." — Shaun, Electrical Subject Matter Expert (former electrical commissioning agent) 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁'𝘀 𝗶𝘁 𝗹𝗶𝗸𝗲 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮𝗹𝗼𝗻𝗴𝘀𝗶𝗱𝗲 𝗽𝗲𝗼𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘁𝗼𝗽 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗶𝗿 𝗳𝗶𝗲𝗹𝗱? Motivating. The culture runs on peer-led training, weekly skill-building, and a genuine expectation that everyone keeps getting better. "Our whole team is leveling up together — writing procedures, driving process improvements, stepping up to lead training. My manager gave me room to sprint. That kind of trust isn't common in this industry." — Gabe, Critical Facility Engineer Look at where this team started and where they are now: building tools, leading AI adoption, stepping into leadership. The common thread was never a degree. It was technical fundamentals, work ethic, and a willingness to keep learning. Meta hires for what you can do and invests in who you can become. If you've got the skills and the drive, there's a place for you here. CFE 🔗 https://lnkd.in/gR_HF6q9 CFE 🔗 https://lnkd.in/g82jhmnR Lead Building Engineer 🔗 https://lnkd.in/g8FCrwcq #MetaCareers #LifeAtMeta #Cheyenne

"A career is not like a single line. You can change, you can shift shape and form, but you will always be you." – Rubi, Clinical Operations Lead When Rubi told people she was leaving her hospital job for research, most of them said she was headed in the wrong direction. Walking away from years of medical training isn't easy, especially in a field where most assume the hospital is the only option. But one friend encouraged her to try it anyway. Today it’s her full-time job at Meta, where she’s a clinical operations lead on our Health Technologies team, working alongside scientists and engineers. Growing up on the border between Mexico and the United States meant living between cultures and languages. That unique experience taught her to adapt quickly, solve problems creatively, and build connections across diverse backgrounds. Rubi credits it for how she works: caring for the people around her, creativity, and resilience. #LatinX #LifeatMeta

We’re excited to introduce the Muse Wonder series with Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, our most capable models yet. Both are frontier models, built to deliver state-of-the-art performance for personal and professional agentic tasks. Two things make Muse Wonder suited for long-running, multi-step work an agent faces every day: -> Active Memory carries your context across conversations and surfaces it when it's relevant. -> Active Focus keeps the models working toward your goal when a task gets challenging, trying alternative approaches, working through blockers, and following through to completion. When you hear "data center," you probably picture rows of servers in a big building. Maybe you're working in one right now. But at Meta, they're built differently — custom infrastructure, real investment in the people who run it, and a direct line between your work and products that billions rely on. We asked our Cheyenne team what sets it apart. 👇 What surprised you most about working at a Meta data center compared to your previous experience? For engineers coming from other hyperscalers and industrial environments, the biggest surprise isn't the technology — it's how quickly Meta trusts you to do the work. 🗣️ "From day one, you have access to all of Meta's tools. No earning your way to basic access. Most places withhold things until they decide they 'trust you enough' — here, you're fully equipped from the start." — Rafael, Critical Facility Engineer · former controls technician in food manufacturing How much ownership do you actually have over your work? Data center operations here is treated as core engineering, not a support function. Our team build tools, automate workflows, and chooses the problems worth solving. 🗣️ "At Meta, you really have the freedom to 'choose your own adventure.' You're empowered to pursue projects you're genuinely passionate about and focus on what drives the greatest impact." — Shaun, Electrical Subject Matter Expert · Cheyenne native, returned home from Oregon What would you say to someone weighing Meta against another data center employer? World-class technology, a team that functions like one, and the autonomy to do your best work all from the comfort of your hometown. 🗣️ "If you've got a strong work ethic, care about doing things right, and want a team that actually feels like one — come talk to us. I came from another hyperscaler, and I can tell you: it's not the same everywhere." — Gabe, Critical Facility Engineer So, what makes Meta different? Ask enough people and the same picture emerges: trust on day one, ownership over real work, and a team that operates like one. That's the difference our Cheyenne team feels every day, and it's why the ones who came from other hyperscalers and industries say the same thing: it's not the same everywhere. Ready to see the difference? updates.text: Engineering simulations are expensive, time-consuming and often require significant manual effort. That's why we're announcing a new collaboration with NVIDIA to bring AI to industrial engineering. The goal? To help enterprises move from AI experimentation to real-world engineering applications, with results they can trust. Mistral brings frontier open-weight models, including Mistral Large 4, and deep expertise in physics AI - powered by the NVIDIA accelerated computing platform, to help companies across a broad range of industries design, simulate and test complex products faster using AI. A central part of the collaboration is to establish open benchmarks for physics AI models and for agentic AI in computer-aided engineering (CAE) and electronic design automation (EDA), across aerospace, automotive and semiconductors. These benchmarks will assess the accuracy of physics AI models, as well as agents' ability to use engineering tools, complete multistep workflows and produce technically correct results - while measuring execution time and computational cost. The combination of open models, accelerated computing and standardized benchmarks is an important step toward making AI a trusted part of engineering.

Today we're launching Voxtral 3: state-of-the-art speech models and a new SDK for building voice agents that can listen, reason, speak, and act in real time. Speech AI has come a long way, but building reliable voice agents remains difficult. They need to understand accents and interruptions, reason about nuanced intent, speak naturally with emotion, and execute multi-step tasks across business systems. All simultaneously. With Voxtral 3, we're bringing these capabilities together: Listen: Transcribe speech with state-of-the-art accuracy across 50+ languages with diarization, context-biasing, and end-of-turn detection. Reason: Interpret nuanced intent and reason through sophisticated requests using conversational context. Speak: Generate expressive speech across 35+ languages and 50+ dialects, and adapt voices to your brand, tone, and personality. Act: Call tools, interact with enterprise systems, and execute multi-step tasks All in one streaming pipeline, available through our EU-hosted API or for self-deployment on your own infrastructure. Available today.

What can large-scale AI models bring to the growing complexity of particle physics? CERN and Mistral join forces to accelerate AI for science and explore this question. We have signed a statement of intent to establish a long-term strategic partnership focused on developing foundation models for scientific discovery. CERN is home to one of the world’s largest volumes of scientific data: around one exabyte (one million terabytes) from the Large Hadron Collider, the world’s largest and most powerful particle accelerator. And with the HL-LHC, expected to begin operation around 2030, the number of collisions is set to increase tenfold. Today, analysing these collisions relies on a chain of specialised algorithms. The ambition: a single Large Physics Model, trained on billions of simulated collisions, designed to support multiple tasks: - reconstructing particle collisions, - identifying particles, - flagging unexpected signals, - evaluating future detector designs. The initial focus is on high-energy physics. But the partnership has the potential to contribute to AI approaches that can serve the broader scientific community, and lead to new scientific discoveries. European excellence in AI and fundamental science, brought together. A step towards a new generation of AI tools.
👋 Welcome to Mistral, New Material . Let’s bring design to mission-critical AI.

updates.text: cargo (libnix) is a fork of cargo with nix built in as a build backend. three releases later 🦀❄️ here is what changed between libnix-1.87.0+v1 and +v3: 🔌 talking to the nix-daemon directly: cargo no longer runs nix build as a subprocess. it speaks the nix worker protocol, so it knows exactly which crate failed, which ones were skipped and which ones came from a binary cache. 📋 build output that reads like cargo: the log renderer is now part of cargo. it prints Compiling / Downloading lines, rustc diagnostics, build logs for failed crates, a correct progress line and the evaluation time. ⚡ parallel builds again: build script flags are no longer read at evaluation time, so nix schedules independent crates in parallel. 📦 crates live in the nix store: in nix mode cargo never downloads a crate itself. the nix-daemon fetches them once (or substitutes them from cache.nixos.org ), and cargo and the nix build share the same store paths. ~/.cargo/registry stays empty. 🧊 flakes via IFD, no vendoring: cargo build write-nix-buildsystem --out-dir generates the build system from the local source. for offline builds the crates.io index is no longer needed: the crate tarballs are computed from Cargo.lock in plain nix and passed in as inputs. no network, no importCargoLock. 🛠️ smaller things: nixpkgs 26.05, cargo --version says +libnix, nix develop works better, and there are clearer safety checks. it's still slower than vanilla cargo, but sandboxed, shared and cached builds plus readable logs make it a pleasant way to build rust with nix. 👉 https://lnkd.in/eDrbN4df #nix #rust #cargo #opensource

updates.text: Every new AI agent used to mean another one-off integration. Every new MCP server, another manual config. Multiply that by a few hundred agents, growing MCP sprawl, and "connect it ourselves" stops being a strategy. Here's what standardizing agent identity actually looks like: 🔹 Register agents with a Client Identity Metadata Document (CIMD) — no more manual credential management per agent 🔹 Browse and connect MCP servers from the Okta Integration Network catalog — not another spreadsheet of endpoints When agents and the tools they connect to are growing faster than any team can manually manage, what does scalable identity actually look like? That's what this is → https://lnkd.in/eg_hDyKP

AI hasn't invented a new threat—it's supercharged the oldest one. And it's now the #1 threat keeping CISOs up at night. The uncomfortable part: most defenses weren't built for this. → 43% of security pros still rely on passwords → Only 36% can tell a human message from an AI-generated one → Basic MFA — passcodes, SMS, simple push — can be phished in seconds In Okta's analysis of ~6,000 social engineering events, organizations that enforced passkeys across sign-in and account management had zero successful account takeovers. 📰 Read the full edition of "Phishing resistance in the age of AI".

Okta is proud to be a part of the NVIDIA OpenShell ecosystem to advance AI security at the infrastructure level. Today, NVIDIA announced the NVIDIA OpenShell Reference Architecture for safe AI agents, which combines controls, accelerated computing, and independent security enforcement in an open architecture. Together, we’re collaborating on how to extend identity, authorization, and governance into the agent runtime, helping sandboxed AI agents operate securely across the full AI stack.

Phishing resistance is a journey, not a setting. Here are 10 steps to up-level your organization: 1. Use Okta Identity Engine 2. Enable phishing-resistant authentication 3. Turn on FastPass or FIDO2/WebAuthn 4. Secure enrollment 5. Protect admin access 6. Protect targeted apps 7. Expand to 50%+ of users 8. Cover every enrollment policy 9. Cover every app 10. Disable weaker authenticators Make a stolen password insufficient to get in. Where is your organization on the path?

Des congélateurs qui montent à 50°C. Des marchandises détruites. Des centaines de magasins impactés. Cette cyberattaque, qui a touché plusieurs enseignes de la grande distribution, illustre une évolution majeure : les attaques ne ciblent plus uniquement les données ou les systèmes d'information. Elles visent désormais des équipements physiques dont dépend directement l'activité. Que révèle cet incident ? Pourquoi ce type d'attaque risque-t-il de se multiplier ? Et que nous dit-il de la transformation des infrastructures connectées ? Dans ce nouvel épisode d'On Décrypte, Laurent Peliks, Partner Cyber, analyse les enseignements de cette affaire et les enjeux qu'elle soulève pour les organisations. 🎥 Découvrez l'épisode.
