Notfall! Dein Account wurde gehackt und nichts geht mehr!🚨😱 Wer kennt die Angst? Wer das verhindern will, muss sich mit Cyber Security auskennen. Genau deshalb finden in dieser Woche die Hamburg Cyber Security Days unter anderem in unserem Headquarter statt. Was 2024 als gemeinsame Initiative von OTTO, bonprix und Jungheinrich gestartet ist, bringt heute Unternehmen, Behörden und Forschungseinrichtungen zusammen, um Wissen zu teilen, Perspektiven auszutauschen und Cybersicherheit greifbar zu machen. Im Fokus des Events stehen aktuelle Entwicklungen rund um KI und Cloud Security, Cybercrime-Trends sowie Medienkompetenz. Dafür geben viele Kolleg*innen Einblicke, wie moderne Technologien sicher eingesetzt werden können, sie geben reale Beispiele, welche Bedrohungslagen Unternehmen heute beschäftigen und geben Tipps, wie wir unseren digitalen Alltag im Job und privat sicherer gestalten können. Es geht nicht darum, Angst zu machen. Wir wollen Wissen aufbauen, Gefahren aufzeigen und lernen, souverän mit digitalen Technologien umzugehen. Denn wer Risiken kennt, kann sicherer handeln. Welche Rolle spielt Cyber Security in eurem Arbeitsalltag?🔐

Wie oft bekommt man die Möglichkeit, einen Teil seiner Arbeitszeit zu nutzen, um sich gezielt zur KI-Expert*in weiterzuentwickeln? Genau diese Chance erhalten 37 Kolleg*innen bei OTTO als Teil unseres neuen GenAI-Enablement-Partner-Programms. Die ausgewählten Kolleg*innen werden gezielt qualifiziert, um Fachbereiche dabei zu unterstützen, KI-Anwendungsfälle zu identifizieren und erfolgreich umzusetzen. Sie schaffen die Voraussetzungen dafür, dass generative KI langfristig Teil unseres Arbeitsalltags wird und dort Mehrwert stiftet, wo er wirklich zählt. Für ihre neue Rolle investieren die Teilnehmenden mindestens 20 Prozent ihrer Arbeitszeit. Sie erhalten umfangreiche Schulungen, wie beispielsweise die 5-tägige, auf unsere Bedarfe angepasste Bitkom-Schulung inklusive Zertifizierung zu Beginn sowie Tool-Schulungen. Dieses Zeitinvestment ist uns wichtig: Wir fördern KI-Kompetenz und geben ihr den notwendigen Raum, um Wirkung zu zeigen und zur Wertschöpfung beizutragen. Die Kolleg*innen können so konkrete Lösungen und Optimierungen mit KI entwickeln. Für uns als Unternehmen ist es ein weiterer Schritt, um die Vorteile von KI sinnstiftend einzusetzen. Wir freuen uns zu sehen, welche Lösungen daraus entstehen.🙌

Was macht deine Arbeit besonders?✨ Diese Frage haben wir einigen Kolleg*innen gestellt. Die Antworten fielen ganz unterschiedlich aus: von tollen Menschen über die Möglichkeit, Veränderungen mitzugestalten, bis hin zu den gemeinsamen Afterworks. Denn hinter jedem Job steckt eine persönliche Geschichte. Und hinter jedem „Why“ ein Grund, morgens gerne zur Arbeit zu kommen. Unsere Kolleg*innen haben ihre Gründe gefunden. Das hier sind sie.👇 Was ist dein persönliches „Why“?

37 Prozent höherer Bestellwert, doppelte Conversion – und viele Gespräche auf der DMEXCO: Gemeinsam mit Google zeigen wir, was unser KI-Shopping-Assistent schon heute leistet. Beim Thema KI ist mittlerweile entscheidender denn je zu verdeutlichen, welchen Mehrwert sie tatsächlich schon schaffen kann. Genau dafür sind wir heute und morgen auf der Kölner Marketingmesse beim Google Stand. Zusammen haben wir nämlich unseren KI-Shopping-Assistenten entwickelt, der Kund*innen dabei unterstützt, Produkte schneller zu finden, Anforderungen zu präzisieren und Kaufentscheidungen einfacher zu treffen. Statt einzelne Suchbegriffe einzugeben, können sie in einem Dialog nachfragen und sich beraten lassen. Unser Assistent wird ständig weiterentwickelt. Gerade haben wir mit Google ein Modell-Upgrade umgesetzt. Jetzt kann der Assistent beispielsweise noch besser Detailfragen zu Produkten beantworten. Dafür greift er auf Informationen aus den Produktdetailseiten sowie auf zusammengefasste Kundenbewertungen zurück und kann so einen Großteil der produktbezogenen Fragen direkt beantworten. Das wirkt sich auch positiv auf die Nutzung aus: Wir verzeichnen immer mehr neue und wiederkehrende User*innen. Wer ist noch auf der #DMEXCO ? updates.text: WebMCP may matter most at large companies where building and maintaining a separate MCP server is difficult to coordinate. It lets existing teams expose website features to agents through the browser. #WebMCP #AI
If you're at AGNTCon + MCPCon this week, be sure to catch Nick's talk, "Authorization After OAuth: Controlling Tools on Hosted MCP Servers You Don't Own"! https://lnkd.in/gmz-kda8

WebMCP could make websites more accessible to people with accessibility needs. But opening your site to agents from anywhere also creates abuse risks. Commercial enterprises may prefer paid, official MCP servers instead. #Accessibility #WebMCP

WebMCP reportedly grew out of an Amazon authorization problem: agents needed to use browser-based auth to access internal tools. The idea was to run the auth system in the browser, send the agent there, and return the authorization result. #WebMCP #AI

Every form on a website may be a WebMCP opportunity. Instead of making an agent slowly fill out fields and click a button, expose the underlying function as a tool. When the agent lands, it can call the function directly. #WebMCP #AI

updates.text: Last year, the p5.js Shared Responsibility Committee (SRC) was formed as a joint decision-making body made of Processing Foundation staff and p5.js community contributors. During its pilot year, the SRC's primary responsibility was deciding how $14,700 could best support the people who build, maintain, document, and teach with p5.js . The funded projects include website accessibility, p5.js v2 tutorials, library maintenance, and p5.strands API. The SRC reinforces a simple idea: sustaining open-source software means investing in the people who care for it. Next year, p5.js SRC will manage the $100,000 grant provided through the Processing Foundation Maintenance Fund, with the core commitment of increasing access to p5.js . Read the SRC’s first-year report: https://lnkd.in/gV-EetEi

To celebrate Processing's 25th anniversary, Processing Foundation is announcing the Maintenance Fund: a permanent endowment that will distribute $200,000 every year to maintain Processing Java and p5.js . Open-source software has historically run on volunteer labor, which means the inequities of time and resources are often reproduced in open-source communities. The Maintenance Fund was created to compensate contributors and resolve technical debt, opening pathways for more diverse contributors to shape the future of these tools. Read more in the latest blog post: https://lnkd.in/g93yARfk

What would Processing look like if it had been created 12 years later? In 2013, Lauren Lee McCarthy initiated p5.js , a Javascript library that brings Processing back to the browser. Three years later, Cassie Tarakajian built the online editor making p5.js even more accessible on the internet. p5.js radically transformed creative coding, opening doors for communities historically excluded from computer science and engineering spaces. Millions of people flooded in. “A Quarter Century of Processing” was presented at Ars Electronica : Negotiating Humanity. Video by Elisa Unger.

The same scene rendered two ways: first on the CPU, then on the GPU. In Processing 5’s Rust R&D, you can draw tens of thousands of 3D shapes simultaneously in the GPU. updates.text: This is me at 11 years old, sporting a red fedora for a photo I thought I'd never use again. It's We Are Red Hat Week. A celebration of our open source culture and an opportunity to look back on our history. The story of our hat [1] is worth a read if you're unfamiliar. This week I've been reflecting on what the hat means to me... Raised in the mountains of Western North Carolina, my education was rooted in Outward Bound and Expeditionary Learning design principles and models at a small public charter school. Curiosity, collaboration, hands-on discovery, and leaning into challenges shaped how I navigate the world. I learned that real growth happens outside comfort zones, that everyone has something valuable to contribute, and that the best work happens when people build things together. In sixth grade, I won a class locker-decorating contest with a photo of myself wearing a red fedora in a contemplative pose with witty thought bubbles above my head. Many years later, I found my way to Red Hat. A company and community anchored in openness, collaboration, curiosity, and meritocracy. Red Hat’s culture of shared ownership, learning from one another, and empowering humans echoes the very educational philosophies that shaped me. To me, the hat serves as a bridge, symbolizing the shared ethos of growth, trust, and collective effort that unites the principles of our Open Organization, Outward Bound, Expeditionary Learning, and how I strive to move through the world. So, maybe my path to Red Hat wasn't accidental. Or maybe the universe just knew that an 11 year old in a red fedora was destined to find her people in open source. Either way, I think the photo makes a pretty compelling case. [1] https://lnkd.in/e9VHMkFy

Tired of false alerts overwhelming your security team? Red Hat researchers and Purdue University engineers have created VEX-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating large language models (LLMs) in assessing software supply chain vulnerability triage. VEX-Bench provides a clear, transparent method to gauge LLMs' ability to accurately reason about vulnerability advisories and perform effective triage. https://red.ht/4xSld1X

It’s We Are Red Hat Week, a yearly celebration of open source culture. Now that I’m entering into my 10th year at Red Hat, forgive me for waxing a little philosophical about what that culture means to me. When I was young, I used to think I had the best creative ideas. I was pushy and a bit arrogant. If things didn’t turn out well, I blamed the execution of others, not my ideas. But as I’ve matured, I see collective participation as an antidote to that creative hubris. Other people’s ideas can be incredibly helpful even if they might slow things down. I’ve long felt there’s a universal war between consolidation and decentralization. From governments to industries to city planning to galaxies, there’s always a push-pull in one direction or the other. I know there are pros and cons to each, but overly centralized systems always seemed more of a problem to me than dispersed ones (maybe that’s just my inherent mistrust of authority). Centralized systems are easier to control, there’s faster decision making and rapid response, and they can eliminate duplicated efforts. But the risk of group think, rigidity and blind spots is really high. Decentralization is messier. There are fits and starts. Abandoned ideas. Arguments. But this is where innovation comes from. When there are a lot of competing ideas, new thinking emerges and the winning ideas can rise to the top. Of course, better outcomes aren’t guaranteed but the potential for solving problems in novel ways is really high. I think one perception about collectivism is that it waters down the brilliance of an “exceptional individual”. There’s a fear that if a genius’s ideas are forced to go through the de-flavorizing machine of a million opinions, nothing truly special or interesting ever gets produced. This is a possible risk, but I think it’s overblown. My time at Red Hat has taught me the strength of open source principles: collaboration, transparency, inclusive meritocracy. I’ve seen over and over how decisions made through collective participation get better outcomes. Someone can have a brilliant idea and someone else can look at it from their unique perspective and to add to it. Or challenge it. We built @s, our own internal agent harness, with Sanity as the backend. It runs more than 70 agents in Slack. Most were built in a single afternoon, and people keep adding new ones. Each part lives where it belongs: → Agents are documents in a Sanity Studio. Anyone can make one in minutes, and iterating is as fast as hitting publish. → Facts live in Knowledge Bases, compiled from sources like our intranet. → Skills live in their own Studio, shared across harnesses. → Tools live in code, merged by pull request. Fix a fact once, and every agent that reads it gets the fix. Retire an agent, and nothing it knew is lost. https://lnkd.in/es8Xescn

I got to build a sandbox for our company’s AI agents to run around with scissors in. Over 300 of my colleagues built their own agents at our all-hands hackathon in Portugal. All the agents live behind @s in Slack. You ask it something, and it figures out which agent should pick it up. No need to remember who does what, and no need to deal with infra, Slack apps, webhooks or tokens every time you want to make a new one We had people building everything from Tamagotchis named after me, which would randomly turn up in Slack to tell everyone I was hungry and ask for food and pets, to more useful agents. One of them even found the root cause of an incident we managed to set off during the hackathon 🫠 @s has been a fun one to build, and because it’s just for m̵e̵, I mean us, I could live on the bleeding edge of frameworks and tech. Even got to use TypeSafe AI Jev for routing! Nowadays I work on Sanity Context, so a lot of this was also getting to use what our team has been building. Seeing teammates put their docs and knowledge into Knowledge Bases, then spin up agents for things they do over and over, has been really cool. And with Context Insights, we have observability into how those conversations actually went. My favourite thing about it is the collaborative aspect: being able to have a convo with your colleagues, and then just calling for your little helper to pick up where you left off. if your agent is missing a tool, you can just ask it to build one and open a PR. Or just ask it to tweak its own b̵r̵a̵i̵n̵ instructions. We wrote about how it works here: https://lnkd.in/e3M2iymU

October’s releases include MCP asset uploads, SAML enforcement for new members, and custom dimensions in Sanity Context Insights. Agents actually requested the MCP asset upload themselves. The Sanity MCP server has a feedback tool agents can use to tell us what’s missing. They asked to upload images and files themselves, without a person opening an upload dialog. Now they can. Doing a migration? Point an agent at the old site and review the result in Sanity Studio, instead of uploading every image yourself. Also in October: Admins can require SAML for every new member. Without this setting, someone could accept an invite with a personal email and end up with an account your identity provider never sees. Now every new member comes through SAML. Insights in Sanity Context accepts custom dimensions, so you can see which group of users gets weak answers. An overall success score can look healthy while one group of users keeps getting bad answers. Custom dimensions show you which group, so you know which content to fix first. 𝗣𝘂𝗹𝘀𝗲 𝗦𝗧𝗧 𝗵𝗮𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗹𝗼𝘄𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗵𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘂𝗰𝗶𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗱𝘂𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘀𝗶𝗹𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲. Silence is everywhere in real calls. A caller pauses to think, looks for a document, gets put on hold, or says, "Let me ask my wife." What should a speech-to-text model output during those gaps? Nothing. But many models invent words from a breath, background TV, or hold music. A made-up "yes" or a repeated sentence can send a call in the wrong direction. On audio with multiple silent gaps, 𝗣𝘂𝗹𝘀𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗱𝗲𝗱 𝗮 𝟲.𝟴𝟱% 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗱 𝗲𝗿𝗿𝗼𝗿 𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲, compared with 14.03% for Deepgram Nova 3 and 40.39% for ElevenLabs Scribe. See how Pulse handles silence. Link in the first comment.

Lightning is the best TTS model for Hindi customer support in Voice Arena’s blind human evaluations. In the demo below, a customer has received his new card, but it has sat unused because he has not activated it. An AI voice agent calls him. The call begins in English, then switches to Hindi as soon as he responds. It patiently walks him through the steps. Those same instructions can sound like a pushy sales call or like someone genuinely trying to help. Wait for the moment he asks for a minute. That is the difference between a call that delivers instructions and one that delivers support.

AI voice agents have one problem. The voice can sound natural, but names and company names are often where they stumble first. A model that hasn’t encountered a name before may mispronounce it based on its spelling. Callers notice, and one mispronounced name can make the entire interaction feel less human. Lightning v3.1 Pro, our text to speech model, is built to handle names, brands and acronyms. Some names need more than a model’s best guess. The pronunciation dictionary lets you define how specific words should be spoken, in plain words, and reuse those pronunciations across calls. Try Lightning v3.1 Pro. Link in the first comment.

We tested Lightning v3.1 Pro against MiniMax Speech-2.8-hd in 22 languages. On Emergent TTS Evals, an open benchmark where AI judges hear two voices read the same text and pick the one they prefer, Lightning v3.1 Pro beats MiniMax in 20 of 22 languages. A voice agent should not sound worse because a caller speaks Greek instead of English. Test Lightning v3.1 Pro in the language your callers speak. Link in the first comment.

updates.text: Attackers were stealing secrets from LiteLLM's GitHub org 11 days before they published the malicious litellm 1.107.0 release. Socket 's Threat Research Team recovered two malicious workflows that ran in BerriAI/litellm on October 10 and October 12. Both runs succeeded. Neither left a trace in the repo's normal history. The technique: • Cut a throwaway branch (ci-tmp-<hex>) from a legitimate recent commit • Push one commit adding .github/workflows/ cache.yml , titled "ci: bump cache config" • Let on: [push] fire in the upstream repo, where secrets resolve to real values • Base64 the secrets, POST them to webhook.site , and append || true so the run always reports success • Delete the branch the same day The October 10 run took six org-level secrets, including a GitHub token and a GitHub App private key. Two days later, a six-job workflow bound five real GitHub Environments to unlock their secrets and took 14 more. No overlap with the first set. Reconnaissance, then collection. Among the 20 secrets: OpenAI, Anthropic, and Bedrock keys, Postgres and Redis credentials, a GitGuardian key for the secret scanner that would surface this activity, and Playwright session state that grants Linear access without a password or MFA. Deleting the workflow didn't erase the evidence. Environment deployment records survive. One is still marked Active, deployed from ref ci-tmp-4d8517. Socket contacted the LiteLLM team as soon as we found this and coordinated publication with them. LiteLLM has since published its own attack-chain investigation. It traces initial access to a key accidentally committed to a public repo in May and never revoked, and says its audit logs link the GH_TOKEN stolen on October 10 to approval of the October 21 release. Thanks to the LiteLLM team for working with us. What we can't confirm: whether October 10 was the start, whether more cycles ran before October 21, or whether the collectors received the data. If you run GitHub Actions, check your environment deployment history and Actions metrics for workflows you don't recognize, especially runs from branches that no longer exist. Full analysis and IOCs by Socket: https://lnkd.in/egxhpxub

🚨 New investigation: Socket found malicious LiteLLM workflows running 11 days before the attack, targeting 20 secrets including GitHub, cloud, and AI credentials. After our disclosure, LiteLLM linked a stolen token to approval of the malicious release. https://lnkd.in/ecYJAe6r

updates.text: Habt ihr schon mal euren Haustürschlüssel verloren? Kein schönes Gefühl, oder? Genau das ist aber einem Achtjährigen in München-Milbertshofen passiert. Der Schlüssel fiel ihm aus der Hand und dann durch eine kleine Öffnung im Schachtdeckel. Weil darauf ein "T"-Logo zu sehen war, bat uns seine Mutter um Hilfe. Unser Telekom-Kollege Jonas, Teamleiter vor Ort, machte sich gleich auf den Weg. Doch der Schacht war blockiert und ließ sich zunächst nicht öffnen. We built three agent memory systems. The most expressive one wasn't the most useful. First, a list of user-scoped facts. Four tools, text snippets, and recall returned everything you had ever saved. Useful for personal preferences, but a poor fit for shared project knowledge. Only a handful of power users used it. Second, a general knowledge graph. Nodes, edges, JSONB metadata, and arbitrary SQL so agents could experiment freely. They got surprisingly good at SQL. They also spent their turns on database mechanics instead of the memory task: integrating one thread summary took dozens of turns. Third, a tree. One table, an ltree path per memory, and tools for working with it. Agents still chose what to remember, where to put it, and how to search. But saving a summary and establishing its place in the hierarchy usually took one tool call. The lesson wasn't that trees beat graphs. It was that flexibility can give agents more work without helping them do the job. Let agents decide what to remember and retrieve. Don't make them invent edge semantics and operate the database to do it. https://lnkd.in/euPzk8Fn #AIAgents #PostgreSQL #RAG #OpenSource

IIoT ingest on PostgreSQL has a failure mode that stays hidden until the day it matters. A remote site drops its uplink. The cause is someone else’s ticket. The backlog is yours. The sensors don’t care - they keep reading for six hours. Then the link comes back and all of it arrives at once. That’s when you find out two things you never tested. Whether those rows land once or twice. And what happens to every other site while that one pushes six hours of backlog through the same pipe. Most teams learn both answers in production. This article shows how to design the reconnect path so neither one surprises you, with the queries to prove it on a staging site first. https://lnkd.in/eYjhg4X2 #IIoT #PostgreSQL #EdgeComputing

Humans hate having to adjust search filters five times in a row. AI agents are great at it—if you give them the right knobs. Over the past year, as we built agent memory and RAG backends at Tiger Data, we kept writing the same retrieval machinery over and over. Today we’re open-sourcing it as searchgres.js . The idea came from watching how agents actually find answers when given raw data instead of complex preprocessing pipelines. Imagine an engineer asking an agent: “Why did Unit 2 drop to 180 MW yesterday afternoon?” 1. The agent searches Unit 2’s logs for that 30-minute window using hybrid search (BM25 + semantic). 2. It spots a shift log referencing dispatch instruction “D-4821”. 3. On its next turn, it searches the dispatch collection for “D-4821”—relaxing the time filter because the instruction might have been issued hours or days earlier. A human rarely searches that methodically because tweaking filters across multiple queries is tedious. For an agent, iterating on search parameters is fast and cheap—provided two things are true: First, the search engine has to let you compose ranking (BM25, vector, or RRF hybrid) with strict filters on hierarchy, metadata, regex, and time in a single query. Second, the database has to pre-filter *inside* the index scans, so your top matches aren’t crowded out by records from the wrong unit or day. Postgres 18 (with pgvector, pg_textsearch, and ltree) gives us all of those primitives in a single database. searchgres.js wraps them—along with a reference MCP server and async embedding workers—into a small TypeScript library (npm install searchgres, Apache-2.0). More on how it works and a runnable example in today’s blog post: https://lnkd.in/gmbUg2E7

The Trimble trailer is on the move. Well, alright, it's always on the move. An Airstream crossing a bridge may not sound exciting, until you realize it's capturing 2 million points a second as it moves, and that the bridge in question is the Golden Gate Bridge. This is possible because of the Trimble MX60 Premium. Its two lasers measure everything around the vehicle in a full 360 degrees. At the same time, its positioning system tracks where the vehicle is as each measurement is taken, so every point can be placed where it belongs in the map. A spherical camera captures the scene from the road to the tops of the towers, and the imagery pops up on screen live as the team drives across. updates.text: Essa semana completei 10 anos de Uber. Essa viagem começou na operação de campo em Belo Horizonte, em 2016, até assumir a cadeira de Diretora-Geral no Brasil. Ao fazer a transição da linha de frente da execução para o desenho estratégico, a principal certeza que carrego é que liderar é um aprendizado diário. Para celebrar esse marco, decidi compartilhar 10 coisas que aprendi – e desaprendi – nesse período: 1. A rua ensina o que os relatórios não mostram. Ter começado com a "barriga no balcão" me ensinou que as decisões precisam funcionar no cotidiano real das pessoas. 2. Vulnerabilidade é sinal de coragem. Aprendi que ser transparente, autêntica e vulnerável constrói confiança. 3. A melhor tecnologia é aquela que "desaparece". A tecnologia mais impactante é aquela que se torna invisível na experiência do cliente. 4. Ideias valem mais do que a hierarquia. A cultura organizacional acelera a experiência quando valorizamos a diversidade de repertório e as boas ideias. 5. Nosso cliente é um ecossistema. Precisamos gerar valor para motoristas e passageiros. A equação mágica está no equilíbrio dessa dinâmica. 6. A estratégia é só o começo. O verdadeiro desafio está em transformá-la em execução. 7. A inovação ganha força no contexto local. Os melhores produtos nascem da união entre escala global e entendimento das necessidades locais. 8. Diversidade não é símbolo, é qualidade de decisão. Ampliar a presença feminina em cargos de liderança é melhorar a nossa leitura do mundo para criar produtos mais aderentes à vida das pessoas. 9. A maternidade e a liderança se potencializam. Viver a minha licença-maternidade de forma integral após assumir o cargo me ensinou a importância de formar times autônomos. 10. Esteja 100% presente. O equilíbrio se mede em intencionalidade. Estar 100% focada quando estou com o meu filho me traz a clareza mental necessária para exercer uma liderança com mais empatia, escuta e assertividade ao retornar ao trabalho. Conectar milhões de pessoas todos os dias é um desafio enorme e um privilégio sem tamanho. Muito obrigada aos parceiros, aos usuários e a todo o brilhante time da Uber que faz essa viagem cinco estrelas acontecer todos os dias. 🚀🚗

updates.text: Driving across Highway 37 in the San Francisco Bay Area on the best of days already feels like driving on top of water. Wheat, one of the world's most widely grown staple crops, provides essential nutrition for billions of people. Looking at my software developer connections to validate this hypothesis/observation. Pls comment if something sounds off, or if you agree on some points in specific: Devs in 2026 are caught between the excitement of what's possible with AI and the anxiety of what it means for their jobs. Many are already overworked, yet expectations continue to rise. Management sees remarkable AI demonstrations online and increasingly expects similar results to be delivered in production, faster and with fewer resources. But while AI can accelerate development, the developer remains accountable for the outcome. AI-generated code cannot be blindly trusted. It still needs to be understood, validated, debugged, and maintained. At the same time, developers face a growing pressure to upskill - even when this is not explicitly stated by management. Beyond their already demanding workloads, they must invest time in learning new AI tools, workflows, and technologies, partly out of genuine curiosity, but also out of fear of becoming less relevant or even losing their jobs. There is real excitement too. Developers can see the extraordinary potential of AI to remove tedious work, accelerate development, and bring ideas to life at a speed that was previously unimaginable. The satisfaction of seeing a working application emerge in minutes rather than days is real. The result is a developer mindset defined by conflicting emotions: - overwhelmed yet ambitious - skeptical yet curious - anxious about being replaced yet genuinely excited about what they can now create. Developers are not resisting AI. They are trying to embrace its possibilities while navigating rising expectations, increasing responsibilities, and uncertainty about their own future.

updates.text: Offensive security has historically been difficult to scale across an entire application portfolio. If an AI-enabled attacker pointed a frontier model at yours today, what would it find before you did? 😲 Swipe to see five principles for closing that gap, and read the full paper here: https://lnkd.in/gQKKGYmB

Attackers don’t need your whole AppSec program to fail. They need one exploitable path. It’s Cybersecurity Awareness Month, and this year’s theme is “Don’t Make It Easy for Them.” I wrote a piece for the XBOW blog applying it to application security. In my conversations with security teams, the same five gaps come up again and again: 1️⃣ Long gaps between tests. Apps ship new features, endpoints and permission changes every week. An annual pentest can’t keep up. 2️⃣ Backlogs with no validation. Thousands of scanner findings, and nobody knows which ones can actually be exploited. 3️⃣ Too little testing of auth, authz and business logic. These are the flaws that matter most, and predefined scans usually miss them. 4️⃣ Fixes closed without checking. A closed ticket isn’t proof. Patching one endpoint can leave the same access open through another. 5️⃣ Rigid testing. Real attackers adapt and chain small weaknesses together. Checklists don’t. The fix isn’t more headcount. Focus testing where change and business risk are highest, prioritize by proven exploitability, and retest every fix. Autonomous pentesting can take human expertise much further without a matching jump in manual effort. Which of these five shows up most in your org? records.about: We’re Zed Industries, a small and passionate team with a vision for building the world’s best text editor—for you, and for your team. Zed isn’t our first editor. It’s the culmination of more than a decade of experience building tools for developers. We created the hackable text editor, Atom, and the pioneering software platform that launched an entirely new generation of desktop apps, Electron. We also built Tree-sitter, an advanced syntax parsing framework used by the most popular editors in the world. Building tools that matter is in our DNA. Now, we’re building something new again with that same drive and a new vision. We believe the best software is handcrafted, with unparalleled attention to detail. We believe software development is better when it’s a shared experience. We believe there’s a better way to write software—and this is just the start of the adventure.

Delta is now in public beta. Delta is a multiplayer environment for coding with agents and reviewing what they build. It keeps the plan, code, terminal output, test runs, and review in one shared thread, so teammates can join with the full context before anything is committed or pushed. Last week, we turned off pull requests in the repository where we build Delta. Reviews now open beside the original thread, carrying the conversation and code with them. An agent generates a guided review of the changes, and teammates can comment in context and talk directly with the people and agents who produced the code. https://lnkd.in/evY5M4Fz

records.name: ZEISS Group
records.about: ZEISS is an internationally leading technology enterprise operating in the fields of optics and optoelectronics. In the previous fiscal year, the ZEISS Group generated annual revenue totaling almost 12 billion euros in its four segments Semiconductor Manufacturing Technology, Industrial Quality & Research, Medical Technology, and Consumer Markets (September 30, 2025). For its customers, ZEISS develops, produces, and distributes highly innovative solutions for industrial metrology and quality assurance, microscopy solutions for the life sciences and materials research, and medical technology solutions for diagnostics and treatment in ophthalmology and microsurgery. The name ZEISS is also synonymous with the world's leading lithography optics, which are used by the chip industry to manufacture semiconductor components. There is global demand for trendsetting ZEISS brand products such as eyeglass lenses, camera lenses, and binoculars. With a portfolio aligned with future growth areas like digitalization, healthcare, and Smart Production and a strong brand, ZEISS is shaping the future of technology and constantly advancing the world of optics and related fields with its solutions. The company's significant, sustainable investments in research and development lay the foundation for the success and continued expansion of ZEISS' technology and market leadership. ZEISS invests 15 percent of its revenue in research and development – this high level of expenditure has a long tradition at ZEISS and is also an investment in the future. With over 46,600 employees, ZEISS is active globally in around 50 countries with more than 60 sales and service locations, around 40 research and development facilities, and 30 production facilities worldwide. updates.text: A polluted river, food safety concerns, and waste in local neighborhoods – these were the topics students explored during the Nairobi Youth Innovation Challenge: “My city. My problem. My solution.” One school group focused on the Nairobi River. What first looked like dirty water revealed a much bigger problem under the microscope: microplastics, textile fibers, and bacteria linked to sewage contamination. The findings helped the students move beyond assumptions and identify possible sources of pollution. Another group investigated waste management in their communities, proposing measures such as color-coded recycling systems and new ways to reuse plastic waste. A third group tested beef samples for sodium metabisulfite, a preservative that was detected in three out of five samples examined during their research. What made these projects special was not that students were given answers. Instead, they learned how to ask questions, collect evidence, and use science to better understand the challenges around them and develop solutions. Through our initiative “A Heart for Science” and in close cooperation with the University of Nairobi, ZEISS supported young people in turning curiosity into investigation and investigation into action. 🌍🔬 #ZEISS #AHeartForScience #YouthInnovationChallenge #Africa #Microscopy

Vision shapes how we experience the world. 👓 It influences how we learn, connect with others, and navigate everyday life. It helps us stay independent, engaged, and connected to the moments that matter. That's why vision and visual health are more than just eyesight. They play an important role in quality of life and well-being. Taking care of our eyes means helping people continue to experience life to the fullest. ZEISS Vision #ZEISS #Vision #VisualHealth #LoveYourEyes #WSD2026

Good vision cannot be taken for granted. Around the world, billions of people live with visual impairment, even though many cases are preventable or treatable. 👁️ Through our Aloka Vision Programme, we work with qualified eye specialists and local partners to bring essential eye care services closer to underserved communities. Over the course of a year, the program reached more than 1.9 million people and distributed nearly 24,000 pairs of glasses, providing better vision for people in need. 👓 ZEISS Vision #ZEISS #Vision #EyeCare #LoveYourEyes #WSD2026 #Innovation #Health

Access to eye care should not depend on where you live. 👁️ In the heart of the Brazilian Amazon, access to quality eye care remains a challenge for many communities. As part of the 58th Expedition of “Expedicionários da Saúde”, we joined efforts to help bring cataract care closer to the Indigenous community of Maués. Through collaboration, medical expertise and on-the-ground commitment, more people can access treatments that may otherwise be difficult to reach. ZEISS Medical Technology #ZEISS #Vision #EyeCare #LoveYourEyes #WSD2026

Good vision can change lives. On #WorldSightDay , we highlight the importance of accessible eye care and the collective effort needed to ensure that more people around the world can receive the care they deserve. 👁️ ZEISS Vision supports initiatives that help expand access to vision care in underserved regions. Through our Aloka Vision Programme, approximately one million people in India and Nepal benefit from access to eye care each year. The goal is a future where good eye health and quality vision care are within everyone's reach. ZEISS Medical Technology is driving innovations in ophthalmology to make eye care more connected, data-driven and accessible. Together with clinicians, healthcare providers and partners worldwide, ZEISS is working toward a future where more people can benefit from better eye health and vision care. #ZEISS #Vision #EyeCare #LoveYourEyes #WSD2026
